app.name: GitHub OAuth App
app.category: Developer OAuth app (not a GitHub App, not a Marketplace listing)

verdict.summary: Registering a GitHub OAuth app is self-serve and takes minutes, with no review step documented for registration. The friction comes later: org owners can block unapproved apps from org data, the 5,000 requests/hour per-user limit caps throughput, and a Marketplace listing is a separate, reviewed process you do not need for your own use.
verdict.hands_on_effort: 30-60 min for your own app; add org approval time if you need org-owned data
verdict.approval_wait: None for registering the app. Org owner approval applies only per organization whose data you access, and its timing is not documented. Marketplace review, if you pursue it, is anecdotally 2-6 weeks.

gates.name: Registered OAuth app used by your own account
gates.unlocks: You register the app and sign in with your own GitHub account to test the flow end to end.
limits: Apps are registered under a personal account or an organization where you have admin access (f1).
Up to 100 OAuth apps per user or organization (f3).
OAuth tokens use the user's 5,000 requests/hour limit (f12).

gates.name: Other GitHub users, within org policy
gates.unlocks: Other GitHub users can authorize your app for their own repositories. Access to org-owned resources depends on each org's OAuth app policy.
limits: No user or install cap for an unlisted OAuth app was documented in the sources read.
Orgs created recently have OAuth app access restrictions on by default; unapproved apps get no API access to private org resources (f14, f15).
Apps owned by a private or EMU org can be signed into only by members of that org (f19).
Expiring tokens: access token lasts 8 hours; refresh token lasts 6 months without use (f6).
gates.time_to_reach: Immediate for personal-account resources; per-org approval for org resources (timing not documented)

gates.name: Open to any GitHub user (no app review); Marketplace listing optional
gates.unlocks: Any GitHub user can authorize the app with no GitHub review of the OAuth app itself. A Marketplace listing is a separate, optional, reviewed step.
limits: Marketplace listing is only offered if the app was set to be installable by any user or organization at registration (f20).
A paid Marketplace plan requires a verified publisher organization; OAuth apps should have at least 200 users (f22).
Listing must provide value beyond authentication (f21).
gates.time_to_reach: Same as Gate 2. Marketplace listing adds a review of roughly 2-6 weeks (anecdotal, not an official SLA).

steps.title: Decide whether you need your own app
steps.detail: Start on Composio's managed GitHub OAuth app to test the flow. Register your own app only if you need your own client ID and secret, your own consent branding, or your own callback URL. GitHub itself suggests a GitHub App instead for fine-grained permissions and short-lived tokens, so check whether that fits before committing.
gotchas: OAuth apps act only on behalf of a user; GitHub Apps use fine-grained permissions (f9).

steps.title: Sign in and open the developer settings page
steps.detail: Sign in to GitHub and go to Settings > Developer settings > OAuth Apps (github.com/settings/developers). The page requires a signed-in account.

steps.title: Choose the owner account
steps.detail: Register under your personal account, or under an organization where you have admin access. If you plan to sell via Marketplace later, note that a personally owned app must be transferred to an organization first.
gotchas: Personal-account apps must be transferred to an org before a paid Marketplace listing (f23).

steps.title: Register the OAuth app
steps.detail: Click New OAuth App. Fill in Application name, Homepage URL (the full URL of your app's website), and an optional description. Paste the Composio callback URL into Authorization callback URL, then click Register application.

values.label: Homepage URL
values.value: Full URL of your app's website (must be a real page you control)

values.label: Authorization callback URL
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: You can enter up to 10 callback URLs at registration; add more with 'Add callback URL' (f4).
Confirm the current callback URL in the Composio dashboard first; the documented default differs between sources (see open questions).

steps.title: Set the token expiry option deliberately
steps.detail: 'Expire user access tokens' is on by default for new registrations. Keep it on if Composio or your code can refresh tokens, which means handling an 8-hour access token and a refresh token that expires after 6 months without use. Uncheck it only if the auth code cannot yet handle short-lived tokens.

values.label: Expire user access tokens
values.value: On (default) unless your auth code cannot refresh

gotchas: Requesting the offline_access scope gives an expiring token pair even if this setting is off (f6b).
Existing tokens stay long-lived until users sign in again after the setting changes (f6b).

steps.title: Turn off legacy wildcard callback matching
steps.detail: Apps with a single redirect URI had wildcard matching enabled by default as legacy behavior. Open the app's settings and check the callback configuration; switch wildcard matching off so only the exact Composio callback URL is accepted.

values.label: Wildcard matching
values.value: Off for the Composio callback URI

gotchas: Wildcard matching is per URI and lets subdomains and subpaths match (f8).

steps.title: Store the client ID and secret
steps.detail: Copy the Client ID and generate a client secret from the app page. Enter both into your Composio custom auth config. Never put the client secret in client-side code.

values.label: Client secret
values.value: Generated on the app page; shown once, store securely

gotchas: Anyone with the secret can use the app's per-app rate limit (f32).

steps.title: Narrow the scopes
steps.detail: Composio's default scope list is broad: repo, user, gist, notifications, project, workflow, codespace. Reduce it to what the integration needs. Requested scopes are shown to users on the authorization form, and users can later grant fewer. Scopes are space-delimited in the authorize URL, and implied scopes are dropped (e.g. user:email is implied by user).

values.label: Scopes
values.value: Minimum set your integration needs; default Composio list is repo, user, gist, notifications, project, workflow, codespace

gotchas: repo grants full access to public and private repositories, including org projects, invitations, team memberships and webhooks (f10).
No scope is documented as needing a separate GitHub review (f11).

steps.title: Run a test authorization with your own account
steps.detail: Connect your own GitHub account through the Composio auth config. Confirm the consent screen lists the scopes you expect and that the callback returns to Composio. If you build your own flow, check that state is verified on return and that PKCE uses S256 (plain is not supported). Authorization codes expire 10 minutes after issue.
gotchas: Exchange the code within 10 minutes (f8c).
PKCE: code_challenge with S256 only (f8b).

steps.title: Test with a second GitHub user
steps.detail: Have a second GitHub account (ideally one that is a member of a restricted org) authorize the app. Confirm personal-account access works. If it fails on org data, the org owner must approve the app.
gotchas: Org OAuth app restrictions are on by default for new orgs (f14).
Private or EMU-owned apps: only members of the owning org can sign in (f19).

steps.title: Get org owner approval where needed
steps.detail: For each org whose data you need, an owner opens Organization Settings > Third-party Access > OAuth app policy, selects Review next to your app, and approves it. Members can request approval, which owners act on. Owners can also disable app access requests entirely.

values.label: Path
values.value: Organization Settings > Third-party Access > OAuth app policy > Review

gotchas: Approval timing is not documented.
Disable app access requests blocks member requests as well (f17).

steps.title: Monitor the rate limit
steps.detail: Track 5,000 requests/hour per authenticated user. Requests from any other app or PAT for the same user share that budget. Apps owned by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud org get 15,000/hour. Use it as the ceiling when sizing a public launch. For device flow, respect the polling interval and the 50 user-code submissions/hour per app limit.
gotchas: Rate-limit increases are granted per OAuth app (f12).

steps.title: Decide on a Marketplace listing (optional)
steps.detail: Skip this for your own use. For a public listing, the app must be installable by any user or organization at registration, and you need a valid publisher contact, description, pricing plan, privacy policy link, support link or email, and value beyond authentication. A paid plan needs a verified publisher organization. Only org owners can create and submit listings for org-owned apps.
gotchas: OAuth apps should have at least 200 users before listing (f22).
The GitHub App manager role does not allow listing submission (f24).

steps.title: Submit the Marketplace listing and wait
steps.detail: Draft the listing, add a pricing plan, accept the Marketplace Developer Agreement, then Submit for review. Expect a human onboarding contact. Review time is not published; one October 2025 community reply said 2-6 weeks. Do not resubmit while under review, since that may restart it.
gotchas: Check that all fields are filled, the public email is verified, and two-factor authentication is on before submitting (community advice).
Resubmitting may restart the review (f27).

requirements.detail: Personal account or an organization where you have admin access.
Authorization callback URL must be the Composio callback URL. Redirect URIs must match the registered host and port exactly; if redirect_uri is omitted GitHub uses the first configured callback URL.
100 OAuth apps per user or organization.
Access token 8 hours; refresh token 6 months without use. Enabled by default for new registrations.
Org-owned resources require owner approval when OAuth app restrictions are on (default for new orgs).
5,000 requests/hour per user for OAuth tokens; shared with other apps and PATs for that user.
Only offered if installable by any user at registration; needs listing requirements, 200 users for OAuth apps, and a verified publisher org for paid plans.

scopes.effect: Full read/write access to public and private repos, including org projects, invitations, team memberships and webhooks. Broadest scope in Composio's default list; drop it unless needed.
Profile access; implies user:email. Narrow to read-only forms if that is all you need.
Access to gists. Request only if the integration uses them.
Access to notifications. Request only if needed.
Access to projects. Request only if needed.
Lets the app update GitHub Actions workflow files. Request only if needed.
Access to codespaces. Request only if needed.

blockers.symptom: Org members cannot authorize the app for org repos, or org data calls return no access.
blockers.cause: Org OAuth app access restrictions are on by default for new orgs, and unapproved apps get no API access to private org resources.
blockers.fix: An org owner approves the app under Organization Settings > Third-party Access > OAuth app policy > Review. Plan for this per org.

blockers.symptom: Requests get rate limited (403/429) once real traffic arrives.
blockers.cause: OAuth tokens use the authenticated user's 5,000 requests/hour limit, shared with other apps and PATs for that user.
blockers.fix: Cache responses, reduce request volume, and treat the per-user limit as the ceiling. Rate-limit increases are granted per OAuth app.

blockers.symptom: Users of a private or EMU-owned app cannot sign in.
blockers.cause: Since June 2025, sign-in to private or EMU-owned apps is limited to members of the owning organization.
blockers.fix: Use a public-owner app for users outside the owning org, or add them to the org.

blockers.symptom: Token refresh fails after 8 hours, or a session expires after months of non-use.
blockers.cause: Expire user access tokens is on by default; access tokens last 8 hours and refresh tokens expire after 6 months unused.
blockers.fix: Ensure the auth code refreshes tokens. Only uncheck the setting if the code cannot yet handle short-lived tokens.

blockers.symptom: Callback returns a redirect_uri mismatch error.
blockers.cause: redirect_uri must match the registered callback host and port exactly.
blockers.fix: Paste the exact Composio callback URL from your auth config into Authorization callback URL, and check wildcard matching is off.

composio.note: Start on Composio's managed GitHub OAuth app to test the flow. Register your own OAuth app only if you need your own client ID and secret, your own consent branding, or your own callback URL. Composio's default scope list is broad, so narrow it before going further. Composio's default redirect URI sits on backend.composio.dev; confirm the exact callback in your Composio auth config before pasting it into GitHub.

evidence.claim: OAuth apps are registered self-serve under a personal account or an organization where the user has admin access.
evidence.quote: You can create and register an OAuth app under your personal account or under any organization you have administrative access to.

evidence.claim: The scopes reference documents repo as full access to public and private repositories (including org-owned projects, invitations, team memberships and webhooks), and lists narrower scopes such as repo:status, public_repo, read:org, and gist.
evidence.quote: Grants full access to public and private repositories including read and write access to code

evidence.claim: The scopes reference does not mark any OAuth scope as requiring a separate GitHub review; requested scopes are shown to the user on the authorization form, and users may later edit their scopes, granting less than requested.
evidence.quote: When setting up an OAuth app on GitHub, requested scopes are displayed to the user on the authorization form.

evidence.claim: Scopes are space-delimited in the authorize URL, and a token saved with several scopes is normalized, dropping any implied by another requested scope (for example, user:email is implied by user).
evidence.quote: discarding those that are implicitly included by another requested scope

evidence.claim: OAuth apps have lower rate limits than GitHub Apps and do not scale; OAuth tokens draw on the user's 5,000 requests-per-hour limit, and rate-limit increases are granted per OAuth app.
evidence.quote: OAuth tokens use the user's rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour.

evidence.claim: Primary rate limit for OAuth tokens is the authenticated user's limit; requests from any other app or PAT for the same user share that budget; apps owned by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization get 15,000/hour.
evidence.quote: requests made by a higher-limit app reduce the remaining budget available for lower-limit authentication methods.

evidence.claim: Device flow has a rate limit of 50 user-code submissions per hour per app, and polling must respect the interval or the app receives slow_down errors.
evidence.quote: there is a rate limit of 50 submissions in an hour per application.

evidence.claim: OAuth app access restrictions are on by default for newly created organizations; while on, members cannot authorize unapproved OAuth apps against org resources and must request owner approval.
evidence.quote: When you create a new organization, OAuth app access restrictions are enabled by default.

evidence.claim: Unapproved OAuth apps get no API access to private organization resources and no privileged create, update or delete actions on public organization resources.
evidence.quote: API access to private organization resources is not available for unapproved OAuth apps.

evidence.claim: Org owners approve an OAuth app from Organization Settings > Third-party Access > OAuth app policy by selecting Review next to the app; members can request approval, which owners then act on.
evidence.quote: In the "Third-party Access" section of the sidebar, click OAuth app policy.

evidence.claim: Org owners can choose whether members and outside collaborators may request approval for unapproved apps; this control reached general availability in January 2026.
evidence.quote: Disable app access requests: Prevent both members and outside collaborators from requesting any apps.

evidence.claim: Privileged OAuth apps are owned by GitHub and are the exception: users can still authorize them even when org OAuth restrictions are on. The privileged list covers GitHub's own clients (e.g., GitHub CLI, Desktop, VS Code), not third-party apps, and the page describes no review path for third parties.
evidence.quote: Some OAuth apps are privileged apps, owned by GitHub, that are granted special capabilities.

evidence.claim: Since June 2025, signing in to a private or EMU-owned OAuth app is limited to members of the owning organization, and internal apps to members of the enterprise.
evidence.quote: to sign into an app, users must now be a member of the enterprise if it is internal, or the owning organization if it's private.

evidence.claim: The registration form asks for application name, homepage URL, optional description, authorization callback URL, an optional device-flow toggle, and the expiring-tokens toggle, then 'Register application'.
evidence.quote: In "Homepage URL", type the full URL to your app's website.

evidence.claim: Marketplace listing is a separate step from registering an OAuth app; the Marketplace section only appears if the app was set to be installable by any user or organization at registration.
evidence.quote: The Marketplace section is only visible if you allowed your app to be installed by any user or organization when registering the app.

evidence.claim: Marketplace listing requirements for every app include a valid publisher contact, a relevant description, a pricing plan, a privacy policy link, a support link or email, working extra links, value beyond authentication, public availability, and webhooks for plan changes.
evidence.quote: Apps must provide value to customers and integrate with the platform in some way beyond authentication.

evidence.claim: A paid Marketplace plan requires the app to be owned by a verified publisher organization, and OAuth apps need a minimum of 200 users (GitHub Apps need 100 installations).
evidence.quote: OAuth apps should have a minimum of 200 users.

evidence.claim: To sell a personally owned app on Marketplace, the app must first be transferred to an organization, which then requests listing verification.
evidence.quote: first you'll need to transfer the app to an organization

evidence.claim: For organization-owned apps, only organization owners can create and submit Marketplace listings; the GitHub App manager role does not grant that.
evidence.quote: only organization owners can create and submit listings in GitHub Marketplace.

evidence.claim: GitHub does not publish a Marketplace review SLA; a Oct 2025 community reply put typical review at 2 to 6 weeks, described as anecdotal.
evidence.quote: the typical review time is 2–6 weeks, but some cases may take longer.

evidence.claim: Submission flow: draft the listing, add a pricing plan, accept the Marketplace Developer Agreement, then Submit for review; an onboarding expert then contacts the publisher.
evidence.quote: Read and accept the terms of the GitHub Marketplace Developer Agreement.

evidence.claim: A community reply lists items to check before waiting on a Marketplace review: all fields filled, a verified public email, two-factor authentication on, and the Developer Agreement signed; it also warns that resubmitting may restart the review.
evidence.quote: Avoid re-submitting: Submitting again may restart the review process.

evidence.claim: The developer settings page github.com/settings/developers is behind a sign-in wall for unauthenticated visitors, so the portal exists but needs a GitHub account.
evidence.quote: Sign in to GitHub

evidence.claim: A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
evidence.quote: A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.

evidence.claim: A client ID and secret can also fetch public data at 5,000 requests per hour per OAuth app; the secret must not appear in client-side code.
evidence.quote: Never include your app's client secret in client-side code

evidence.claim: Up to 10 callback URLs can be entered at registration, with more added through an 'Add callback URL' control.
evidence.quote: You can enter up to 10 callback URLs.

evidence.claim: 'Expire user access tokens' is enabled by default on new registrations; it can be unchecked if the app's auth code does not yet handle short-lived tokens.
evidence.quote: Expire user access tokens is enabled by default.

evidence.claim: Expiring tokens: the access token expires after eight hours and the refresh token expires after six months without use; using the refresh token returns a new access and refresh token pair.
evidence.quote: The access token expires after eight hours, and the refresh token expires after six months without use.

evidence.claim: Apps can opt in per sign-in by requesting the offline_access scope, which returns an expiring access token and refresh token even if the app is not configured for expiring tokens; the registration setting can also force expiring tokens for all new tokens, but existing tokens stay long-lived until users sign in again.
evidence.quote: When you request the offline_access scope, you will receive an expiring access token and a refresh token even if your app is not configured to use expiring tokens.

evidence.claim: Short-lived tokens are enabled by default for new OAuth app registrations (August 2026 changelog); apps with a non-supporting SDK can disable this while updating.
evidence.quote: Short-lived tokens are enabled by default for all new applications.

evidence.claim: When redirect_uri is sent it must match the registered callback host and port exactly and reference a subdirectory of the callback path; if omitted, GitHub uses the first configured callback URL.
evidence.quote: If left out, GitHub will redirect users to the first callback URL configured in the OAuth app settings.

evidence.claim: Wildcard matching on a callback is opt-in per URI and lets subdomains and subpaths match; apps with a single redirect URI had it on by default as legacy behavior, now visible and switchable off.
evidence.quote: Apps with only one redirect URI have wildcard matching enabled. This is a legacy behavior of GitHub

evidence.claim: The web flow accepts PKCE: code_challenge with code_challenge_method S256 is supported (plain is not), and the token exchange takes a code_verifier.
evidence.quote: Must be `S256` - the `plain` code challenge method is not supported.

evidence.claim: The authorization code expires 10 minutes after it is issued, and the state parameter should be checked on return to protect against forged requests.
evidence.quote: The temporary code will expire after 10 minutes.

evidence.claim: GitHub's own guidance says to consider a GitHub App instead of an OAuth app, since OAuth apps act only on behalf of a user while GitHub Apps use fine-grained permissions and short-lived tokens.
evidence.quote: Consider building a GitHub App instead of an OAuth app.

open_questions: Composio callback URL: the toolkit metadata shows https://backend.composio.dev/api/v1/auth-apps/add as the default redirect URI, while the probe used https://backend.composio.dev/api/v3/toolkits/auth/callback. Confirm the current value in your Composio auth config before registering it on your app.
No documented user or install cap for an unlisted or unreviewed GitHub OAuth app was found. The only documented cap is 100 OAuth apps per owner.
Ordinary OAuth app registration showed no review step in the docs read. I did not confirm whether homepage URL or privacy policy is checked at registration.
Whether Composio's managed app requests exactly its default scope list at authorize time is unverified.
Whether Composio's auth flow refreshes expiring tokens automatically is unverified. This determines whether you should keep 'Expire user access tokens' on.
Refresh-token rotation: the docs say a refresh returns a new access and refresh token pair, but do not explicitly state that the refresh token rotates on every use.
GitHub's OIDC support for OAuth apps is unconfirmed; the discovery page was not fetched.
Org approval timing is not documented and depends on each org owner.
Marketplace review timing has no official SLA; the 2-6 week figure comes from one October 2025 community reply.
